Experimental results indicate that QP-WNet produces higher quality signals with lower computational requirements compared to the standard WaveNet. The code and demo can be found on the authors' GitHub repository: https://github.com/jmjjian/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the most widely-used technique, have become an essential part of our daily lives as consumers. The success of CF stems from its ability to leverage the behaviors and preferences of like-minded users for recommending unexplored items. Recent advancements in CF involve enhancing its user-based and item-based core principles to address emerging challenges. Researchers have proposed an array of CF methods, each targeting specific issues, such as the effectiveness, computational efficiency, and scalability of recommendations. Despite significant progress, managing the inherent complexities of user preferences, sparse rating data, and item popularity remains a significant hurdle for CF in providing high-quality suggestions. This paper presents an innovative solution to address these challenges by integrating the concepts of CF and Biclustering, an unsupervised data mining technique. The proposed Bicluster-based CF method groups users and items into cohesive subsets while preserving their unique behaviors and preferences for recommending undiscovered items to like-minded users. The computational efficiency and the effectiveness of this approach are demonstrated through comprehensive experiments using real-world datasets, which show promising results and outperform state-of-the-art CF methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

This research examines how various solar magnetic features influence the spectral patterns observed on the Sun, using Sun-like activity to inform the analysis of exoplanet transit missions. We utilized the HARPS-N instrument to gather high-resolution spectra of the Sun and found that solar magnetic features leave distinctive imprints on the data. We tested several candidate activity indicators and determined that the most reliable ones are based on specific spectral lines or line combinations. We also developed a new metric that accurately gauges solar magnetic activity from the spectral data and found it to be particularly effective. Notably, this metric along with the other two indicators exhibit correlations with solar faculae areas and can potentially be used as proxies for photospheric magnetic field strength. Furthermore, we found that solar spots primarily affect the spectral patterns at very short cyclic phases. We utilized a solar model to determine that spots primarily influence the spectral data at cyclic phases near the minimum, while faculae have a greater impact on the patterns at cyclic phases around the peak. We compared the best spectral patterns to a comprehensive database of solar spectra across various solar cycles and found that the top three patterns accurately capture the dynamic behavior of solar cycles for both cycles studied and historical data.

A new technique has been proposed to differentiate Majorana from other zero-energy peaks using a distinct tunneling spectroscopy method that incorporates resistive electrodes in a measurement circuit. The method relies on the removal of non-Majorana peaks via high-resistance connections, whereas Majorana peaks remain unaffected, thus enabling accurate identification. The method's effectiveness was validated through numerical simulations of a common tunneling spectroscopy measurement using a setup with a zero-energy peak and ohmic leakage.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending the original theoretical framework of shadows introduced by Harp, which models subspaces within geometric contexts. This expanded framework, referred to as the theory of $\mathbb{K}$-shadows, achieves this by subsuming the original theory as a specific instance. The $\mathbb{K}$-shadows framework itself is encompassed within the broader theory of shadows when a certain distribution property is enforced. Furthermore, the theory of shadows is shown to be invariant against a specific type of morphism, thereby establishing its bicategorical nature.

We've developed a novel approach to transfer learning in image processing, using a predefined style extracted from a collection of images, to create customized tone-mapped versions of input images, regardless of their brightness. Our algorithm identifies a key component - a mapping function, known as 'M', that converts an input image into a scaled version, using a predefined network architecture, allowing for efficient training and optimization. To acquire the preferred style, an additional network, called 'S', is introduced, which uses multiple iterative backward-branch networks to isolate distinctive features in a set of reference images, while a central forward-branch network, trained end-to-end, captures the unique characteristics of these images. Once the style is extracted, it can be applied to achieve consistent results on input images, using a weighted average mechanism to balance the effects of the mapping function and style components. Our approach is flexible, enabling the use of pre-trained models to streamline the optimization process and reduce memory requirements. Furthermore, it permits the introduction of external constraints, such as total variation regularization, to be incorporated into the network for improved performance. Our experiments showcase the efficacy of our method in producing high-quality, visually appealing images, with an evaluation on 2D and 3D medical images, as well as a detailed analysis of the impact of external constraints.

This report outlines the details of the winning entry in the CVPR 2022 Aqua-Queensferry Tidal Current Estimation Competition, specifically describing the proposed method's objectives, overall strategy, and the specific algorithm used to estimate tidal current velocities.

Selectively influencing the direction of snowfall flakes is theorized to occur as a result of interactions with atmospheric turbulence. This process is presumed to happen through turbulence-generated structures that cause flakes to navigate in specific areas, potentially increasing the efficiency of snow accumulation on surfaces. To verify this phenomenon, researchers simulated the behavior of a small snowflake within atmospheric turbulence using numerical modeling, revealing its rapid rotation in response to turbulence forces. Selective "sweeping" of the snowflake in certain regions was consistently observed, aligning with theoretical expectations. These simulations provide evidence for the proposed mechanism of directed snowfall flakes in the atmosphere.

Our proposed system presents an integrated framework that ensures autonomous robot movement is guided by a dynamic and adaptable plan generated through deduction. This plan effectively navigates around obstacles in a constantly changing environment by continuously reforming the robot's plan in response to shifting environmental conditions. We have developed a sophisticated formal system to represent and logically derive these navigation plans. Additionally, we have defined an active version of this formal system that actively searches for and refines relevant information to support the robot's navigation. We have further demonstrated the feasibility of implementing this formal approach on a real robot using an inference engine based on resolution theorem proving. Experimental studies have validated the efficacy of our approach in maintaining stable and goal-directed movement even in the presence of uncertainties in the environment.

Three-dimensional time-projection chamber experiments aim to detect rare events associated with sparse data. Current reconstruction methods are limited by the random nature of these events, leading to inefficient use of computing resources. To address this issue, a new approach involves a Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) that enables the direct mapping of 3D coordinates from sparse ionization patterns. By training the BCAE with reconstructed data, it can accurately predict corresponding 3D coordinates from the original ionization patterns. This autoencoder's inverse transformation can then be used for both new data sets, reducing the need for computational processing. To achieve this, a BCAE-based strategy is proposed to pre-process the data, followed by a projection step. This method was validated using simulated data from the NEUTRINO-4 experiment, resulting in significantly reduced CPU time for each event.

In Finzi's gravitationally interacting dark matter model, dark matter's self-force varies according to the square of the mass distribution's gravitational potential, resulting in it being similar to a collisionless fluid with a density proportional to the square of the mass distribution's gravitational potential. Researchers have observed that this model's dark matter behaves in a manner reminiscent of a dark halos. To gain insight into the model's core characteristics, scientists have analyzed the distribution of galactic cluster mass profiles in the Finzi model, employing the $\Lambda$CDM model's halo mass function as a reference for comparison. Additionally, they have computed the average gravitational potential and mass profiles within a fixed radius in groups of simulated galaxies, and found that these profiles conform to the Navarro-Frenk-White profile when adjusted for mass.

A type of complex object called a convex geometric hypergraph, comprising a set of specific complex shapes, sparks curiosity in researchers. By examining a particular instance of this complex object, known as a 1-3 geometric hypergraph, based on specific geometric constraints, an important question regarding its potential for containing certain numbers of shapes is investigated. According to a fundamental theorem in similar fields, a specific lower limit exists for the maximum number of shapes within a particular instance of this complex object. However, a particular instance, featuring three shapes, challenges this lower limit, highlights a potential area for improvement in existing research, and points out a potential area for further investigation, namely the potential for shape saturation.

To study particle yields, researchers have developed theoretical transport models. These models, such as the isothermal Boltzmann model and the quantum molecular dynamics model, can effectively predict yields but have limitations. Specifically, the isothermal Boltzmann model performs well for light systems but struggles with heavier systems, while the quantum molecular dynamics model provides accurate results but is computationally intensive. As a result, developers have created new versions of these models to improve accuracy and simplify computations. For example, the isothermal Boltzmann model with the Weisskopf parameterization and the quantum molecular dynamics model with the primary decay option aim to address these issues. Using the $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V system at an incident energy of 4.95$A$ GeV, researchers have evaluated and compared these new model versions with each other and existing models. Interestingly, the modified models demonstrate promising potential, particularly the 3D quantum molecular dynamics+primary decay model, which accurately matches calculated and measured data for both proton and alpha particle yields. Furthermore, the 3D quantum molecular dynamics+primary decay model exhibits strong agreement with measured transverse mass distributions, further validating its effectiveness.

A comprehensive model for navigating utilizing a brain map is achieved through a novel algorithm inspired by the brain's structure of the zebrafish. This model effectively simulates decision-making processes in the fish's behavior. To apply this algorithm to a robotic system, we constructed a mobile robot incorporating sensors and a display screen featuring a representation of the surroundings, referred to as a 'brain map.' The robot's autonomous navigation is based on a motivational system, which directs the robot's exploration and learning. Upon receiving a signal indicating the presence of a target, the robot's goal-oriented system triggers its navigation. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the robot's ability to navigate through a complex environment.

Onco-immunology, the intersection of cancer research and immunology, strives to comprehend how the immune system interacts with tumors and to develop immunotherapies. Specifically, a particular type of tumor reaction known as the tumor microenvironment (TME) hinders the immune system's ability to fight colon cancer through suppression mechanisms. The ultimate goal of treatment for colon cancer arising from an ideal TME type, classified as type-1 (effective), should be to eradicate the tumor. We employed a probabilistic framework to model this situation, using two key variables: the level of tumor control achieved by the immune system and the intensity of the tumor growth. The dynamic interaction between these variables was represented by a system of stochastic differential equations, influenced by both deterministic and random factors. The desired treatment outcome corresponds to the probability distribution of the system's long-term trajectory, which can be estimated by analyzing the associated Fokker-Planck equation. The goal is to find an optimal control strategy, governing the release of cytokines, that leads to the long-term desired probability distribution, while also minimizing costs associated with their release. The resulting optimal treatment will provide the best possible chance of long-term survival.

The increasing demand for wireless services is outpacing the available spectrum. Nanoscale communications via Device-to-Device (D2D) technology have the potential to fill this gap. In this study, a new scheduling approach for D2D networks is presented, which optimizes throughput while minimizing interference. Unlike existing methods, this approach takes a comprehensive power control strategy that accounts for both transmit power and receive power. A complex non-convex optimization problem is simplified and an iterative algorithm is devised to solve it efficiently. Furthermore, a deep learning method is developed to solve the scheduling problem in real-time. Unlike traditional optimization techniques that require channel state information, this approach works with short-time frequency-division multiple access channel states. Experimental results show that the deep learning method achieves similar performance to the iterative algorithm while being applicable in real-time.

This research demonstrates that helicity is preserved in solutions to the compressible Euler equations under certain conditions. Specifically, for a barotropic fluid with a convex pressure law and a potential temperature function that satisfies a certain smoothness criterion, when the velocity field belongs to a specified function space and meets a non-degeneracy condition, a renowned existence theorem applies and enables the calculation of a unique solution. Furthermore, a renowned existence theorem was used to show that helicity is preserved in solutions to the compressible Euler equations.

The researchers, focusing on the Davey-Stewartson II equations in a specific special case, studied how a nonlinear wave interacts with a barrier in both theoretical and practical terms. Their analysis involved both a specific limit and numerical methods. In the process, they discovered an unexpected feature: as one key parameter increases, the behavior of another, related parameter, shifts from complex to purely real. This distinct change was numerically confirmed. Interestingly, this associated parameter's real value partakes in a behavior that becomes more pronounced with higher values of the mentioned parameter. Moreover, this feature has been observed in both scenarios where the wave interacts both positively and negatively with the barrier.

The advancement of gravitational wave detectors is expected to enable the detection of more massive black hole mergers within larger regions of space. Future developments will likely enable the observation of massive black holes in areas of limited disruption: just a tenth of a parsec from their host stars. Within these close distances, initial falling orbits may exhibit residual eccentricities resulting from their disturbed initial conditions. According to existing estimates, a radius of disruption of 0.01 parsecs should result in minimal eccentricities, less than 35 parts per ten thousand. We have conducted a more precise analysis of the problem, accounting for the effects of gravitational waves on the motion and incorporating the properties of the main sequence stars they are derived from. The outcome indicates significantly lower eccentricities than previously predicted: less than one part ten thousand. This implies that, if a major source of binary black hole mergers in the future is found to be within a certain radius, it is likely the result of a different origin, such as a different type of stellar environment, rather than the result of stars in the area causing disruptions with limited eccentricity effects.

Achieving high average power, high temporal coherence, and long coherence lengths is crucial for many scientific and applications at X-ray wavelengths.  A novel "seed and amplify" approach utilizes a free-electron laser oscillator to generate a highly coherent X-ray flux through a series of FEL oscillation rounds.  By incorporating a short undulator in the feedback loop, it is possible to obtain extremely low noise, high flux levels of tens to hundreds of MW, and coherence lengths exceeding 100 $\mu$m within the 10-100 nm spectral range.  This technique may find applications in coherent X-ray sources, nonlinear spectroscopies, and other areas.

In the event of a spread of influence within a connected network, such as a social network or urban system, detecting the initial point of incidence is of utmost importance for informed decision-making purposes. However, conventional methods that systemically analyze data in search of anomalies are often hindered by the unpredictable nature of incident origins. A novel approach presented in this research involves utilizing an adaptive algorithm to pinpoint multiple incident locations based on spatial and temporal timestamp data of events. The method assumes that events sharing a common incident origin exhibit similar temporal patterns, thus grouping correlated events enables the identification of incident locations. A simulation-based evaluation demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed approach in accurately determining incident points, particularly when multiple incidents occur simultaneously and when limited temporal data is available.

Research on shock wave collapse remains a pressing issue in astrophysics, influencing various celestial phenomena including supernovae, stellar winds, and cloud collisions. A comprehensive review of shock collapse is presented, focusing on sudden collapse and gradual collapse determined by critical density ratios and adiabatic indices. We also examine numerical solutions and develop an online tool to facilitate the analysis of shock wave collapse in changing density media.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence (AI) in everyday life has led to a surge in the need for its explanations to build user trust. While research on explainable AI (XAI) has focused on technological aspects, little attention is given to the requirements that underpin good explanations. This paper proposes a novel approach that places XAI's user needs at its core. By examining the needs of various stakeholder groups, it outlines potential requirements for clarifying AI's decision-making processes. These requirements can inform the development of appropriate XAI solutions, such as transparent mechanisms or personalized justifications, thus serving as essential input for practitioners and further research.

This study presents UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset of histopathological samples derived from the UniBiopat dataset. Originally designed for the Hep2Index project, UniToPatho has been adapted for use in learning to classify and evaluate abnormalities in colorectal polyp histopathology. The dataset comprises 13,524 annotated histopathological samples, each paired with corresponding histopathological image data. The training subset contains 10,524 samples, with an additional 3,000 samples in the test subset, and 1,000 in the validation subset. The team's approach to extending the baseline model involved incorporating multiple convolutional neural network architectures, ultimately achieving a 50% relative improvement in adenoma grading accuracy using the combined scores of the two architectures on the public leaderboard. The public leaderboard also reveals that the team's method outperformed the baseline in terms of mean adenoma grade-closure, with a 0.10 increase in the combination's score and 0.06 in the individual architectures' scores. The dataset and accompanying documentation can be accessed at the project's website: https://github.com/igulano/UniToPatho.

Data protection has always been a primary concern for data storage and transmission. In this context, we focus on the fundamental limits of data security for information theory. Specifically, we're investigating the theoretical bounds of data leakage in a source encoded for zero error. Our analysis views data leakage as a graph-based concept, where distinct vertices represent the outside and inside networks. From a security perspective, an edge exists between these vertices if there's a connection allowing data transmission from the inside to the outside network. Utilizing graph theory, we determine the maximum data leakage for any given vertex cut in this graph, essentially mapping the data security issue to a standard graph theory problem. To find the optimal data leakage rate, we apply the max-flow min-cut theorem. Furthermore, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving zero data leakage, drawing parallels with classic information-theoretic problems.

Deep learning techniques are now widely used for enhancing synthetic aperture radar (SAR) image quality, but they struggle to handle under-sampled data due to their black-box nature. A new model, MrSARP, has been proposed to overcome this challenge by utilizing a hierarchical framework that incorporates prior knowledge of the radar imaging process. This approach consists of two layers: PolSARP, which utilizes polarized SAR data to generate a full-resolution image, and a Bayesian network that utilizes a prior distribution learned from real-world SAR data to refine the image. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of MrSARP in producing high-quality SAR images, with the model's transparency also making it more explainable.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant incorporates variational principles and classical optimization elements to solve complex optimization issues. One method to improve its outcomes is to increase the variational circuit's fidelity, which can be accomplished by enhancing its parameters. A novel technique called Bayesian Enhancement, which employs a Bayesian routine to generate additional amplitude measurements to refine parameter adjustments, is presented in this paper. Through simulated and actual findings, we demonstrate that this method leads to better outcomes and greater convergence speeds when combined with Variational Bayesian Optimization, whereas conventional approaches like Markov Chain Monte Carlo fail to achieve similar results due to non-amplitude-related issues, in contrast to amplitude-related issues we successfully overcome. A Python code for this method is also provided on GitHub.

This research explores the intersection points of two ellipses, focusing on their regional variations within different combinations of ellipse orientations and positional relationships. By introducing a set of standard coordinates centered on the cell containing these intersection points, we establish a simplified model for the intersection regions. Based on this framework, the paper establishes a universal system for classifying intersection points and their associated regions, along with precise coordinate equations that define these areas for specific cases where the cells' major and minor axes align either directly or at 45-degree angles. To complete the analysis, this study derives the equations for the boundary curves of these intersection regions.

The concept of q-training is typically applied in a static setting, where the goal is to identify the optimal query strategy for a specific data collection. However, in an ongoing data framework, new information becomes available in real-time and decisions must be made immediately without the benefit of complete knowledge. Moreover, existing methods often require a substantial amount of knowledge about the data and are difficult to apply in real-time. In contrast, we examine the q-training problem in an ongoing data context and propose an algorithm that adapts to changing circumstances in real-time.

Recent theoretical studies have suggested the presence of quantum magnetic systems that exhibit both chiral and nematic properties. Chiral order arises from the natural skewing of certain orbital orientations on triangular lattices, whereas nematic order is derived from the directional properties of electrons within this skewing background. Chiral nematic order can be stabilized through an equilibrium state that favors a specific spin arrangement, known as the N\'eel state. Conversely, non-equilibrium conditions may lead to the occurrence of antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. These phase transitions and the associated correlations between neighboring sites are explored in detail within the extended triangular-lattice Hubbard framework. Magnetic oscillations, an approach used to investigate the stability of nematic phases, reveal that these phases become more stable as they move further away from half-filling. Furthermore, in a specific range surrounding half-filling, both nematic and chiral phases coexist with antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. Critical temperature analysis in two-dimensional systems shows that nematic phases exhibit power-law behavior with temperature, whereas in three-dimensional systems, this behavior is seen to be consistent with finite-temperature stability. These findings are consistent with experimental data from materials such as CuFeCh3($x$)=$$_x$$(Ni$_{1-x}$Cu$_x$)F$_2$(H$_2$O)$_6$($Et$_4N)_2$ with triangular arrangements.

Accurate vertebrae localization is a complex and time-consuming process that's usually done by experienced radiologists. Current automated methods involve labor-intensive data preparation, such as manual landmark placement, which isn't feasible for large datasets. We've developed an automated system that localizes and identifies vertebrae from CT scans with minimal manual input. Our novel approach involves spinning and resizing the CT image to match the natural spine curvature, followed by vertebrae detection and enhancement. To refine the identification process, we've incorporated spatial and anatomical constraints. Our method requires only the manual marking of the L1 vertebra, making it suitable for large-scale clinical use. Evaluation trials demonstrate that our automated system produces results comparable to those of human radiologists.

A statistical approach known as random thermodynamics can effectively describe the dynamic behavior of complex polymer systems and similar substances. The core of this method involves mathematical functions, referred to as Edwards-Anderson order parameters or current functions, which are used to develop expressions for key physical properties of interest. In cases where interactions between substances are influenced by electric currents, additional considerations must be taken into account to ensure the mathematical expressions remain consistent under changing variables. In this study, a rigorous mathematical examination of this issue is conducted, and the findings are applied to a specific scenario of interacting polymers that undergo a process known as phase separation.

This research paper investigates how relative quantum homologies of compact Lagrangian submanifolds in symplectic geometry change under certain geometric transformations. Specifically, it proves that relative quantum homology remains invariant under combinations of handle attachments and handle deformations. Additionally, it is demonstrated that this relative quantum homology is a rational homology class that can be computed using Morse theory and is an essential tool for studying the embeddedness and intersections of Lagrangian submanifolds.

Two piezoelectric crystals, positioned near a resonant frequency, are used as acoustic wave sources and detectors, arranged in a way that allows them to interact with each other's resonant vibrations. By applying an external electric voltage, one crystal generates a directed acoustic wave, which is then detected by the other crystal and converted back into an electric signal. Studies have shown that when the two crystals are very close to each other, typically within the wavelength of the resonant frequency, they can exchange acoustic energy with high efficiency, effectively acting as an acoustic waveguide.

We explore a unique optical system consisting of a confined exciton-polariton assembly, situated near a resonant cavity and driven by coherent laser light. The exciton-polariton assembly behaves autonomously as a self-organizing entity, exhibiting complex patterns of movement and interaction, which can be studied using techniques from condensed matter and laser physics to manipulate and understand its collective properties. Due to the system's self-organization capabilities, it displays distinct characteristics unlike simpler external drive systems. The exciton-polariton assembly shows signs of a complex, non-ordered state before transitioning into a highly ordered state at a critical threshold of excitation, a phenomenon commonly observed in the collective behavior of living organisms. The exciton-polariton assembly's collective properties emerge from the interplay of the exciton-polariton's coherent flow and the localized interactions within the assembly's internal structure. Using numerical simulations, we can control the exciton-polariton assembly's behavior by adjusting the excitation cavity's boundaries, thus modifying the assembly's microstructure and exhibiting two distinct types of critical behavior.

The disintegrating planetesimal K2-22b has been found to have altered characteristics across six years of observation. Notably, its 13-day orbital cycle has been accompanied by an overall increase in brightness. Observations using the Large Binocular Telescope have detected a notable rise in the planet's smaller-grain size, suggesting larger particles, potentially as large as those found on other disintegrating exoplanets. Data obtained through the phase-contrast imaging technique have revealed an estimated mass loss rate four times higher than previous observations, indicating accelerated loss. As a result, the predicted time left for K2-22b to exist has been reduced to around 1.3% of its initial projected lifespan.

We demonstrate a coherence property of the Milnor fiber of a point on a projective variety, derived from the flatness of a specific locus. This coherence property enables the expansion of the Milnor ring through a set of generators related to its minimal generators. Furthermore, this coherence property leads to the completion of the Milnor ring as a finitely generated $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$-algebra.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform data analysis library developed in C# for.NET frameworks. It provides data analysts and scientists with a rich set of tools to efficiently work with data, incorporating popular algorithms and methodologies within a user-friendly API. Daany aims to balance both comprehensive functionality and clear readability, facilitating seamless integration into existing.NET projects.

I re-evaluate the commonly held view that Galileo opposed philosophy to demonstrate the central role mathematics played in his overall intellectual endeavor. Mathematics wasn't a separate field from philosophy; rather, it was an essential component of it. As a philosopher, Galileo employed mathematical methods not just to gather data, but also to address fundamental metaphysical and physical issues. Mathematics facilitated his natural philosophical inquiry, and he utilized it to counter opposing views, often ones supported by the Church. By incorporating mathematical considerations into his philosophical writings, Galileo was able to challenge Dobson's interpretation, and his own stance on mathematics wasn't an isolationist position, but an integral part of his philosophical vision.

This research explores how Saha's ionization affects gases during the initial universe's non-cosmological recombination period, revealing unexpected effects. Through mathematical analysis, we demonstrate that radio waves are capable of traversing interstellar distances and, upon reaching Earth, can be detected as X-ray flashes. Additionally, we find that in a universe undergoing non-cosmological recombination, gas clouds exhibit non-Gaussian ionization patterns, which in turn influence the radiation field. Furthermore, we show that this unusual ionization can impact the primordial deuterium abundance, while also potentially producing detectable anisotropies in the Cosmic Microwave Background using specific observational methods.

The integration of Magnetohydrodynamics and Particle-In-Cell models allows for simulations of collisionless plasmas. A novel MHD-PIC code was developed to quantify magnetic island formation and merging in a collisionless environment. The study utilized this code to simulate magnetic reconnection and island merging within a collisionless setting. By adjusting numerical parameters, the simulation resolved both electron and ion thermal velocities, enabling an investigation of their influences on magnetic island merging. Furthermore, the simulation demonstrated the role of the Larmor radius in determining the reconnection rate and identified a critical time for magnetic island merging.

This study introduces Amanuensis, an innovative information retrieval system that personalizes user queries by adapting to their search history before suggesting relevant keywords to enhance their search. Amanuensis's query refinement functionality is based on the principle of adding prefixed wildcards to retrieve intended results more effectively. Furthermore, the researchers evaluated several complex documentation systems, including our own Amanuensis, as part of a broader examination of text manipulation strategies, and explored the interplay between these systems in a specific search context.
